title: Kernel latency surface mapping: Nsight deep-dive and mitigation experiments
body:
Summary:

This note captures a focused Nsight Systems + CUDA graph investigation we ran to explain persistent per-SM utilization skew and intermittent tail-latency spikes on the production microbatching path. Goal was to map the "latency surface" across kernel-launch phases, quantify the contribution of capture/launch ordering, and validate mitigations that are safe to roll out in Dedicated and Private deployments.

High-level finding (TL;DR):
- SM utilization imbalance is driven primarily by host-side launch serialization during KV-cache warmup and by CUDA-graph capture semantics that coalesce launches in a way that amplifies SM wavefront alignment drift.
- Simple mitigations (staggered launch offsets + stream reordering + cudaStreamBatchSubmit where available) reduce tail latency 35-48% in our microbatch experiments and raise average SM utilization from ~62% -> ~80% on A100 80GB nodes for our test model.

Context and why this matters:
- Symptoms observed in prod: periodic 99.9th latency spikes when a route is cold or after a model switch; persistent SMs showing high idle time while a subset saturates. Offline load tests demonstrate same pattern with synthetic workload that replicates prefix lengths.
- We suspect launch ordering + kernel-phase overlap (attention vs FFN) interacts with our batching horizon and NVLink/KV-cache prefetch to produce phased waves that leave many SMs idle between dense launches.

Environment and repro setup:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (DGX-like node), PCIe config standard.
- Driver/CUDA: NVIDIA driver 525.xx, CUDA 11.8 runtime.
- Nsight: Nsight Systems 2022.5 for timeline captures; ncu for per-kernel metrics.
- Model: open-weights-32B-v2 transformer (decoder-only), typical server config: microbatch=16, sequence=512 (prefix-heavy distribution), kv-cache enabled.
- Capture commands (example):
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=nvtx --output=tmp/trace --sample=none --cpucopy no \n    -- \n    ./serve_bench --model open-weights-32B-v2 --microbatch 16 --seq 512
- NVTX markers inserted around: batch_enqueue, kv_prefetch_start/finish, attention_kernel_start/finish, ffn_kernel_start/finish, reduceAndCopy.

Observations from timeline and metrics:
1) Kernel-launch serialization windows
- Nsight timeline shows regular dense bursts where multiple kernels are queued from a single host thread with small deltas (~1-3us) between launches. This correlates with long stretches of idle time on 40-50% of SMs while other SMs handle dense waves.
- Root cause: single-threaded host-side sequencing on the capture path during prefix materialization and KV prefetch. When the capture path uses CUDA graph capture mode, host launch ordering is recorded and replayed, preserving the dense burst pattern.

2) CUDA Graph capture coalescing effect
- Graph capture removes per-kernel dispatch latency but also flattens the temporal spacing between event boundaries. On replay, we see stronger wavefront alignment — which _improves_ throughput in steady-state but exacerbates SM-skew on non-uniform workloads (prefix-heavy requests).
- Evidence: comparing captured vs non-captured traces, captured replays have 18-25% higher instantaneous occupancy variance (per-SM standard deviation).

3) KV cache prefetch and stream contention
- Prefetch copies (async cudaMemcpy) and attention kernels sometimes compete for L2 bandwidth and cause micro-pauses. When prefetch is launched on the same stream as attention, it contributes to serialized bursts. Moving prefetch to a dedicated stream reduced serial bursts in the timeline but introduced cross-stream synchronization points that must be handled carefully.

Quantitative metrics (representative):
- Baseline (no mitigations, captured graphs): average SM utilization 62%, per-SM stddev 22%, 99.9th token latency 420ms
- Mitigation A (staggered launches: host adds micro-offsets to kernel dispatches): avg util 74%, stddev 14%, p99.9 290ms
- Mitigation B (dedicated prefetch stream + cudaStreamBatchSubmit where supported): avg util 78%, stddev 11%, p99.9 250ms
- Mitigation C (experiment: persistent-threaded kernel prototype to maintain warp warmness across microbatches): avg util 81%, stddev 9%, p99.9 220ms (prototype only; memory model implications flagged)

Mitigation experiments (details):
- Staggered launch offsets: Insert micro-sleeps / schedule offsets per-microbatch in host code ( calibrated between 0.5-3us). This breaks the worst-case alignment and is cheap to implement. Cons: increases host CPU jitter and complicates latency budgeting.
- Stream reordering: Place large copies and KV prefetch ops on a separate high-priority stream. Use cudaStreamPriority to ensure attention kernels preempt long copies. Observed reduced serialized windows on timeline captures.
- cudaStreamBatchSubmit: On supported drivers (testable via driver query) use this API to submit many small work items as batches to the GPU driver — reduces driver-side overhead and allowed us to preserve spacing while maintaining throughput.
- Persistent kernel prototype: implement a persistent threaded decoder kernel that accepts microbatch vectors instead of launching per-token kernels. This reduces launch overhead and allows internal scheduling to avoid SM starvation. Memory and correctness complexity high; need deeper safety review.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Staggering improves skew but adds host-side timing dependence; in low-latency routes this could slightly increase median latency. Need route-specific rollout (canary on background/standard tier first).
- Moving prefetches to a separate stream requires careful synchronization to avoid reading stale KV entries; must retain NVTX markers and strict correctness tests.
- Persistent kernels change memory ownership and error modes; implementation risk is non-trivial for Dedicated/Private where kernels must support more hardware variants.

Recommended rollout plan:
1) Short term (safe, 1-2 sprints):
   - Canonical fix: move KV prefetch and large host-to-device copies to a dedicated high-priority stream. Add NVTX markers and automated Nsight capture in CI smoke tests (owner: Avery Patel, JIRA-ENG-1423).
   - Implement small staggered offset (0.5-1us) as an opt-in config per route (owner: Jordan Kim, PR #271).
2) Mid term (2-3 sprints):
   - Add detection for CUDA Graph capture path and selectively enable spacing-preserving replay (or disable capture for cold-start-heavy routes). Add telemetry to surface per-route SM variance.
   - Experimentally enable cudaStreamBatchSubmit where driver supports it; gate on driver version.
3) Long term (Q2+):
   - Evaluate persistent-threaded kernel approach as opt-in for high-throughput dedicated pools. Start with an internal prototype and run correctness/mem-safety audits.

Action items:
- A. Add per-route SM-variance telemetry to console (metric: per-sm-util-stddev over 60s window). Owner: Marta Rodriguez. Target: 2027-02-01. Linked JIRA: JIRA-ENG-1508.
- B. Ship PR that moves prefetch to dedicated stream + NVTX markers in serving runtime (PR #271). Owner: Jordan Kim. Target: 2027-01-18.
- C. Add nightly Nsight capture job for a small synthetic workload to detect regressions (owner: Liam O'Connor).
- D. Document driver/version gating and cudaStreamBatchSubmit availability in ops runbook.

Open questions / notes for follow-up:
- We need to benchmark on multi-GPU NVLink configs (current repro is single GPU); inter-GPU KV coherence could change behavior.
- How do quantized kernels (int8/int4 fused implementations) change wavefront density timing? Early experiments suggest slightly tighter kernel durations which may increase alignment problems; follow-up required.
- Consider adding an adaptive micro-offset algorithm that measures per-route variance and tunes the offset automatically.

Attachments and artifacts:
- Linked PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/271
- Proof-of-concept Nsight traces stored in gs://redwood-nsight/kernel-latency-surface/ (internal)
- JIRA tickets referenced above.

Conclusion:
This suite of Nsight captures and small experiments showed that host launch ordering and CUDA-graph capture semantics are amplifiers of SM utilization skew. We have cheap, low-risk mitigations that materially reduce tail-latency and increase average SM utilization. Next steps are to land the prefetch-stream PR, enable per-route telemetry, and run canaries in Dedicated pools before expanding to Private customers.

Notes to reviewers:
- Trace files are large — use Nsight Systems with the provided NVTX markers to reproduce the visualizations.
- I've left raw nsys export commands and a small python repro harness in the PR linked above.
